full_judgment:
2. The plaintiff-appellants filed the suit for declaration of tittle. The plaintiffs alleged that the land described in schedules A and B to the plaint belonged in Khash to Dhaka Nawab Court of Ward Estate. Subsequently the plaintiffs took settlement of the lands of schedule A and B for salami of Taka 2,273.50 paisa and Taka 4,057.50 paisa respectively in the year 1353 BS after fulfilling all the formalities required by the estate. The plaintiffs were in possession of the lands of both the schedules openly and adversely against all others since the year 1353 BS. The plaintiffs by different kabalas sold out all other lands except the lands described in schedule C to the plaint. Now the plaintiffs are in possession of the C Schedule land which formed the subject matter of the suit. The men of defendant i.e. the Government have set up clam to the C schedule land as forest land and sought to posses the same in spite of the fact that the Government never acquired the said land which bear no forests and to which the plaintiffs had acquired indefeasible title by virtue of lease and possession for more than 25 years. Illegal claim set up by the Government-defendant had cast a cloud upon the title of the plaintiffs giving cause of action for the suit. 

 3. The defendant contested the suit by filing written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit land as well as A and B schedule lands were forest land in the khas possession of the Dhaka Nawab court of ward Estate. All the forest land under Nawab Estate within the suit village Choota Kaliakor PS Savar were acquired under East Bengal Private Forest Land and accordingly the Collector, Dhaka invited application from the public under section of the Act to put forward their claim for the land if any, and the same was published in Dhaka Gazette dated 6th May, 1994. None including the plaintiffs put forward their claim within the specified time and consequently CS Plot Nos. 11,14, 22, 32, 88, 129, 138, 161, 170, 171, 189 and 191 of the said mouza comprising an area of 137.34 acres of land were decided to be constituted as a reserve forest. A notification to that effect bearing No. 3125 was published in the Dhaka Gazette dated 13th April, 1955 and since then the suit land and the other lands of the aforesaid plots constitute a reserve forest in possession of the forest department of the Government. It is further contended by the defendant that the plaintiff's story of lease from the Dhaka Nawab Court of ward Estate is absolutely false. The plaintiffs had fabricated some false documents in collaboration with the officials of the Court of Ward Estate and they had no possession of the suit land. The suit was therefore, liable to be dismissed. 

 6. The High Court Division held that the settlement of the suit land with the plaintiffs was not approved of by the Chief Manager of the Nawab Estate and therefore Ext. 2 and 2(a) would not confer any title upon the plaintiffs. It also held that the plaintiffs having not taken any steps to lodge any claim under the then Private Forest Act. 1949, the discretionary relief under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act cannot be granted to the plaintiffs. 

 7. In disposing of the petition for leave to appeal, this Division held that the plaintiffs case was dismissed by the trial Court and the High Court Division because they failed to prove their own case of settlement. The trial Court found the documents of the plaintiffs as fabricated. The lower appellate Court did not reverse the finding of the trial Court as to the fraudulent nature of the documents but additionally found that the settlement was not granted by the competent authority to grant settlement, namely, the Chief Manager of the Dhaka Nawab Court of Ward Estate. In the face of these findings, it was held, "it does not lie in the mouth of the plaintiffs to challenge the constitution of reserve Forest. They have not proved their own case of settlement." 

 10. The material question in revision before the learned judge of the High Court Division was, whether the vital documents of settlement of the plaintiffs were properly construed by the court of appeal below. A construction of document is of course, a mixed question of law and fact and the same having not been properly construed by the lower appellate Court the High Court Division was within its competence to reverse that finding after giving cogent reason. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division found that the document creating lease in favor of the plaintiffs having been executed by a person having no lawful authority the same would not confer any title to the plaintiff. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division found that the salami receipts were not granted by the Chief Manager of the Dhaka Nawab Estate who was competent to approve the settlement and consequently the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division after reversing the finding of the lower appellate Court held that by dint of Ext. 2 and 2(a), salami receipts no lease was granted in favor of the plaintiffs. Thus it cannot be said as has been argued by Mr. SR Pal, learned Advocate for the appellants, that the lower appellate Court having reversed the finding of the trial Court on giving valid reasons the same cannot be interfered with by the High Court Division and this Division ignored its own established practice in this regard by accepting the finding of the High Court Division. 

 12. The defendant Government has also filed Ext. B to show that all the Forest Land under Dhaka Nawab Court of Ward Estate within the suit village Chotto Kaliakoir, police station Savar were decided to be acquired under Private Forests Ordinance, 1949 and accordingly the Collector, Dhaka invited applications under Section 22 of the Act to put forward any claim for the land and the same was published in the Dhaka Gazette dated 6th May 1954. CS plot Nos. 11, 14, 22, 32, 88, 19,138,161,170,171,189 and 191 of the said mouza comprising an area of 137.34 acres of land were decided to be constituted as a reserve forest. Section 22 of the Private Forest Ordinance 1959 as amended from time to time provides for issuance of proclamation by Forest Settlement Officer. Sections 23-24 and 25 provide for inquiry and power of the Settlement Officer to modify the said proclamation. An appeal is provided under section 26 of the Ordinance. Under section 26 (4) also revision is provided before the Board of Revenue. After exhausting all these procedures the acquisition of Forest land will be complete. There is no material on record to show that the plaintiffs filed any objection or claim under the Private Forests Ordinance, 1954 either.
